items.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
items.author: raphlinus
items.content:
Raph Levien, November 21, 2026

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

Text layout and accessibility infrastructure is basically solved

One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of and Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

That said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Optimization opportunities

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

  • Be bold. Now is the time. Rust UI has the potential to deliver vastly higher performance than the status quo.
  • Build on solid foundations.
  • Use well-defined specs when available.
  • Find ways to work well with open source. Work with upstream but don’t spam them with slop PRs.

Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post.

Five theorems, proved in the submission's . Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (, , DirichletCharacter.LFunction, ) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
  ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis

2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at , where the L-function has its pole.

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

"GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

As a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit ), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. the archive's directory was at /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean on every build machine, so each source file was passed to Lean as /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean/src/<Module/Path>.lean
  • How the original build was done, and the rebuild that checks it. The original build ran on cloud machines without a sandbox, and compiled each file by calling directly with the same inputs supplies (module name, package name and the lakefile's options), not through . All the kernel checks above were run on the export from that build. We then repeated the build on a separate machine with inside a bubblewrap sandbox: no network, the source tree read-only, only writable, the archive downloaded afresh from the author's site, and Mathlib's files checked against the official cache first. The export made inside that sandbox is byte-identical to the published one, so every check on the published export applies to it.
  • The per-file hashes depend on the build directory, and one module is not deterministic. In Lean v4.33.1 a compiled file stores each linter message together with the absolute path of its source file. Of our 175,187 compiled files, 98,219 contain the path /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean/src/…; the other 76,968, including , contain no path. So can be reproduced only by a build whose source tree is at /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean; elsewhere, only the files of modules that emit no linter messages should match. The sandboxed was run at that same path, and 175,186 of its 175,187 files are byte-identical to our manifest. The exception is Formalism/LocalToGlobal/SiegelLatticeTheory/CokernelGLCounts/RankPointCounts/LocModel.olean: same size, different contents. Recompiling that one module six times on one machine with identical inputs gave one output four times and the other twice, and those are exactly the two hashes in the two manifests. The two outputs differ in 38 bytes: the name of one bound variable in , an equation lemma that Lean generates automatically the first time a proof asks for it. Two adjacent theorems in the file both ask for it, Lean elaborates theorem bodies in parallel, and the lemma takes that variable's name from whichever theorem gets there first. Bound-variable names play no part in kernel checking, so the two files are logically the same. The export is not affected, and the export from the sandboxed build is byte-identical to ours: an export contains only the declarations that the five theorems depend on, and is not one of them, because the proofs that caused it to be generated do not refer to it. We checked that this name does not occur in the export. Had a proof on the dependency path referred to such a lemma by name, two builds could have produced exports with different hashes, although every check would still have passed on either. Compiled single-threaded (), the module gave the same output six times out of six. A ten-line file with no imports reproduces the behaviour: on Lean v4.33.1 and v4.34.1 it compiles to two different outputs with and to one with ; on v4.36.0 it gave one output in 40 runs. The same race, with the first caller's options in place of its names, was reported as Lean issue #15498 and fixed by pull request #15499, first released in v4.36.0. That change also removes this behaviour: the file gives two outputs on the nightly builds of 7 and 8 October 2026 and one output in 40 runs on those of 9 and 10 October and on the toolchain built from the pull request alone. Because of this module, the sha256 of the whole manifest file is not reproducible even at the same path; compare file by file.
  • A passing check shows that the formal statements, as written in Lean against Mathlib's definitions, follow from the three standard axioms according to the kernels used. It relies on those kernels and on Mathlib's definitions being what they are intended to be.

We introduce , a multiple-choice text benchmark for LLMs where individuals with unspecialized (high school) knowledge outperform SOTA models. SimpleBench includes over 200 questions covering spatio-temporal reasoning, social intelligence, and what we call linguistic adversarial robustness (or trick questions). For the vast majority of text-based benchmarks LLMs outperform a non-specialized human, and increasingly, exceed expert human performance. However, on SimpleBench, a non-specialized human baseline is 83.7%, based on our small sample of nine participants, outperforming every tested LLM, including today's top model, Claude Fable, which scored 81.9%. While we expect model performance to improve over time, the results of SimpleBench confirm that the memorized knowledge, and approximate reasoning retrieval, utilized by frontier LLMs is not always enough to answer basic questions just yet.

items.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
items.author: soheilpro
items.content:
Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦

  • 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable
  • UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display

What I thought was interesting#

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The driver and flow control#

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

But the upload was always fine#

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:

Frames/s reaching the Mac behind the display

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…

So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:

Frames/s reaching the Mac

Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:

$ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])"

# old adapter (RTL8156B)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3

# new adapter (RTL8157)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7

# bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

items.title: MRAM Basics: How Magnetic Memory Is Replacing Embedded Flash
items.author: giuliomagnifico
items.content:
Most embedded engineers know the limits of flash memory well. Writes are slow, and every write needs an erase first. Each cell survives only 10,000 to 100,000 write/erase cycles.

Magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) removes most of these limits. It stores data as a magnetic state, not as trapped electrical charge. Microcontrollers built on 22 nm and 16 nm processes now use it, because embedded flash isn’t practical at those nodes.

This article explains how MRAM works, why flash stopped scaling, and what changes for firmware.

The Bit Is a Magnet, Not a Charge

A flash cell stores a bit as electrons trapped on a floating gate or in a charge-trap layer. An MRAM cell stores it in a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ). This is a stack of two ferromagnetic layers, usually a cobalt-iron-boron alloy (CoFeB), separated by a magnesium oxide (MgO) barrier about 1 nm thick.

As illustrated in Figure 1, one magnetic layer, the reference layer, has its magnetization fixed during manufacturing. The other is the free layer. Its magnetization can point in the same direction as the reference layer or the opposite direction. These two states are called parallel and antiparallel. This is a nonvolatile memory because both states are stable without power.

A basic implementation of a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) bit cell. Image used courtesy of Lam Research.

Reading relies on tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR). The barrier is thin enough for electrons to tunnel through, and they tunnel more easily when the two layers are parallel. The antiparallel orientation is typically two to three times higher resistance than the parallel orientation.

A sense amplifier compares the cell current against a reference and returns a 1 or a 0. That gap is small, which is why MRAM designs typically run error-correcting code (ECC) on every read.

Most embedded MRAM uses spin-transfer torque (STT) for the write operations. The write circuit drives a large current through the junction, and the electrons become spin-polarized as they pass through a magnetic layer. They carry that angular momentum into the free layer and set the magnetization direction. Reverse the current and the bit flips back. The bit cell is one access transistor and one MTJ, as shown in Figure 2.

An MRAM cell consists of a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) bit cell in series with an NMOS transistor.

Flash Hits a 10 V Wall at 28 nm

Embedded flash scaling didn't stall because the transistors became too small. It stalled due to voltage. The oxide for the flash memory must be roughly 8 nm to 10 nm thick, or the stored charge leaks away. Pushing electrons through oxide that thick takes about 10 V, but a 22 nm logic process runs its core below 1 V. Creating the 10 V on chip requires charge pumps and special high-voltage transistors, and neither shrinks with the rest of the logic.

Manufacturing makes it worse. Integrating a flash cell into a CMOS logic process adds 9 to 18 extra masks at 28 nm, according to figures reported by Semiconductor Engineering. The flash cell also does not integrate well with FinFET transistors. As a result, embedded flash is widely available down to 28 nm but rare below it.

MRAM avoids these problems:

  1. The MTJ sits between metal layers, above the transistors (Figure 3).
  2. MRAM works with planar, FD-SOI, and FinFET CMOS processes.
  3. The MRAM write voltage is close to normal logic levels.
The MTJ bit cell integrates easily with the NMOS word line transistor. Image used courtesy of Lam Research.

Is MRAM Endurance Really Infinite?

One limitation of Flash memory is that it wears out. Each program and erase forces charge through the oxide. The oxide accumulates damage until it can no longer hold charge adequately.

MRAM switching moves no atoms and stores no charge, so the magnetic layers themselves do not wear out. That is how Everspin’s EMxxxLX Industrial STT-MRAM can specify unlimited read, write, and erase operations for the supported life of the product. Those devices also support 10 years of retention as a minimum.

TSMC specifies one million cycles for its 16 nm embedded MRAM. The write current stresses the thin MgO barrier, so designers of embedded memory must trade endurance against retention at high temperature. TSMC's 16 nm FinFET MRAM is therefore specified for one million cycles with 20-year retention at 150°C. This is still 10 times the endurance of flash.

MRAM is also faster than flash. TSMC reports average write pulses slightly over 30 ns and 6 ns read times for a 22 nm design tuned for speed. And there is no erase step. NXP says its 16 nm MRAM can update 20 MB of code in about 3 seconds, a job that takes flash about 1 minute.

Table 1 compares STT-MRAM with NOR flash.

Table 1. Typical characteristics of embedded NOR flash and STT-MRAM.
Trapped electrical chargeMagnetization direction of the free layer
Microseconds to program; milliseconds to erase a sector
About 10 V or more, from charge pumpsClose to logic supply levels
Oxide wear, charge leakageStrong magnetic fields, high temperature

Your Firmware Gets Simpler, With Three New Checks

Think about what your flash driver does today. It erases a whole sector, waits, and then programs it page by page. An MRAM driver simply overwrites data in place, and it can change a single word without needing to erase and rewrite its neighbors. Therefore, over-the-air updates finish faster, so your device spends less time half-updated. Production-line programming speeds up too.

Data logging benefits even more. With flash, your firmware buffers records in RAM, manages sector erases, and spreads writes with wear leveling. A power failure during a long erase can still corrupt data.

With MRAM, each record goes straight to its final address in microseconds. The reduced time means a corresponding reduction in the likelihood of losing data due to a power failure.

While 1 million write/erase cycles sounds like a lot, don’t skip the math when designing your application. Imagine an energy meter that saves its running total once per second. If you write to one fixed address in an embedded MRAM, you will exceed 1 million cycles in under 12 days.

If you design your code to rotate across 1,000 different addresses, then the same memory lasts about 32 years. If you are writing only once an hour, a million cycles would allow your MRAM to operate for more than 100 years.

Before you commit to an MRAM design, you should make three datasheet checks that flash never asked of you:

  1. Solder reflow characteristics

Let’s take a look at magnetic immunity first. A strong external field can disturb an MTJ, so vendors specify a maximum. TSMC reports ten-year immunity above 1,100 Oe at 25°C for its 22 nm MRAM. Compare the rating with any motors, magnets, or large inductors near your board.

Second, examine the retention specs at your maximum operating temperature, not at room temperature.

Third, solder reflow. If you program parts before assembly, the data must survive the reflow oven. TSMC's 22 nm MRAM retains data through six reflow cycles, but its speed-tuned variant gives up that capability.

If your part passes all three and your write rates fit its endurance, MRAM is the simpler memory to design with. Below 28 nm, embedded flash will rarely be on the menu anyway.

MRAM stores data as a magnetic state, so it avoids the high voltages and extra masks that stopped embedded flash at 28 nm. It writes fast, needs no erase step, and has far higher endurance than flash. Before you pick a part, check its endurance, magnetic immunity, retention at temperature, and solder reflow rating.

items.title: Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit
items.author: geden
items.content:
After a voyage of more than eight years and 6bn miles, a joint European-Japanese space mission has arrived at Mercury and is preparing to swing into orbit around the tiny, barely explored world.

The BepiColombo mission will become only the second in history to circle the first rock from the sun and the smallest planet in the solar system when flight controllers fire the spacecraft’s thrusters on Saturday and send it into orbit.

For researchers, the €1.6bn (£1.4bn) mission is the best hope yet of understanding how Mercury formed so close to the sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what makes up the frozen ice that lurks in the planet’s permanently shadowed craters.

“We’re very excited, it’s been a long wait,” said Prof Emma Bunce at the University of Leicester, who has worked on the project for 20 years.

Getting to Mercury poses unusual difficulties. Because the planet is near the centre of the solar system, spacecraft accelerate under the sun’s gravity and must spend much of their time braking to avoid shooting straight past. “It’s a very complex and challenging mission,” said Bunce, the principal investigator on an instrument called the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer, or MIXS, which will analyse the geochemical composition of the planet’s surface.

It will be some months before scientists can start observing Mercury. In early December, the spacecraft will separate into two orbiters, one European, the other Japanese, which will manoeuvre to different polar orbits around the planet. Science operations are due to start in April next year.

The European probe, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter or MPO, will map the planet’s surface and composition at high resolution, and study Mercury’s interior to shed light on its unusually large core. Its Japanese partner will measure the planet’s magnetic field and its sodium exosphere, the extremely thin layer of gas and atoms that surrounds the planet. Mercury is only 50% larger than the moon but has four times its mass. One question the mission will explore is why the rock is so dense.

Prof Geraint Jones, the lead project scientist on BepiColombo at the European Space Agency, said anticipation of the scientific results had kept everyone enthused during the spacecraft’s eight-year journey.

“We’re expecting to learn a huge amount, bringing more powerful instruments on two spacecraft to study all aspects of the planet – its interior, surface, and the space around it,” he said.

Mercury is a planet of extremes. The tiny world takes 58 Earth days to rotate on its axis, meaning any given spot on the surface can experience daylight for three months and then night-time for three months. It is little more than a third of Earth’s distance from the sun, at only 36m miles. In the day, ground temperatures reach 450C while at night they drop to -180C.

Jones said: “As well as cameras covering a wide range of wavelengths to study the surface, we’ll be ‘tasting’ the gases around the planet, sensing the magnetic field, probing the interior with ultrasensitive instruments, and mapping the shape of the whole planet with a laser.”

The spacecraft are expected to orbit Mercury for about three years, after which they will run out of fuel, lose altitude and ultimately slam into the surface. “Sadly, they are not coming back,” said Bunce.

items.title: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
items.author: Ricapar
items.content:
An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.

The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.

It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.

I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.

From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.

Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?

And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?

I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.

As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.

Type at the prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off.

The whole harness runs on the PC. is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS.

Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.

From a sentence to a running program

One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.

The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.

WarGames, written on the XT

ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a under 10 KB.

Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:

Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in , finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.

That call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB:

And this is what Claude made of it:

Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do.

Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s language.

A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy.

Claude works on the machine through these:

Look at the system, list directories, read files as text or hex, find text across files
, , , , Create and change files; replaces one piece of a file in place
Run DOS programs and batch files and read back what they printed, up to twelve commands in a call, with a screenshot on request
Read and write memory and I/O ports
PC speaker music and coloured CP437 art
, , Its own notes, kept in

A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in . All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one.

Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories:

On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks first. F3 turns it off.

Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too.

Any model, mid-conversation. lists the providers in and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works.

The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on.

has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads.

api anthropic claude-opus-5-5 round=1 ttft=2750 total=4015 up=165 len=1784 stop=tool_use in=2 out=221 cr=5543 cw=739 th=cont
relaunch: program 61.5 s, CLAWDOS away 82.3 s

flowchart LR
    subgraph DOS["IBM PC XT (8088, 640K, CGA)"]
        direction TB
        subgraph APP["HARNESS.EXE"]
            direction TB
            UI["Chat screen"]
            LOOP["Agent loop<br/>Messages API requests, SSE and JSON,<br/>history on disk"]
            TOOLS["Tools<br/>files, search, DOS programs, screenshots,<br/>memory and ports, speaker"]
        end
        NET["mTCP + packet driver"]
        APP <--> NET
    end

    TUNNEL["TLS tunnel<br/>copies bytes"]
    API["Claude Messages API"]

    NET <-->|"plain HTTP"| TUNNEL
    TUNNEL <-->|"HTTPS"| API
IBM PC XT 5160: 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K, CGA. A PicoMEM card supplies the disk (an image on microSD), WiFi as an NE2000, EMS and a battery clock
13,000 lines of C and C++, built with Open Watcom for the 8086 instruction set
, 176 KB, the whole harness. , 29 KB, the launcher you type
FreeDOS 1.4 with mTCP for TCP/IP
The Claude Messages API, streamed: tool use, images, prompt caching, message threads
A tunnel on another machine, , or . It copies bytes between a plain port and . It can also hold the API key, so the key never touches the PC’s disk
A program ClawDOS runs gets 200K beside the harness, or 450K when the harness steps out
31 boot tests in DOSBox-X against a mock API, unit tests that run on DOS, and runs on 86Box’s 8088

docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back.

You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is .

python3 scripts/setup-tools.py          # fetch the compilers, FreeDOS, mTCP and the emulators
echo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... > .env
python3 scripts/build.py                # build/CLAWDOS.IMG, a bootable disk
python3 tunnel/tunnel.py                # the TLS tunnel, on port 8443
python3 scripts/run86box.py             # boot an IBM PC XT

At the prompt, type .

No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type and send .

build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type . Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG).

Stop a reply, or clear the input
Effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max

Setup in full, real hardware, the image updater, other providers, every setting
What ClawDOS sends to the API and expects back
HARNESS.EXE: the chat screen, the turn, the tools
CLAWDOS.EXE, the launcher
The pieces: screen, console, network and HTTP, the API request writer and stream parser, JSON, history, the tool executors, screenshots and the PNG encoder
The TLS tunnel and the mock Messages API
What goes on the disk: the manifest, the system prompt, the tool schemas, the skills, the tests
Build, disk image tools, the emulator runners and test harnesses
DOSUNIT.EXE, the unit tests that run on DOS

ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its ). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it.

Your personal information may be transferred to and processed in the United States and other countries where Backblaze and its service providers operate, which may have data protection laws that differ from those in your jurisdiction.

items.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says:

A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing.

In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.

First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:

  • Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic.
  • It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so.
  • It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions.
  • It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in .
  • It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal.

Importantly, Clojure is a very Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.

I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight of generating and evaluating new Perl code on the fly, which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp way".

Pragmatism and hard-won experience

The designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of industry experience. I strongly recommend watching some YouTube videos of talks by leading Clojure developers. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful:

Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it.

There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from , hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.

Sequences and laziness for powerful in-language data processing

Applications that process and extract useful bits of information from large datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent. What we want in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a successful approach).

Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book:

All the functions used here are built-ins, including the  macro. This
code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat
more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers.
The clojure.spec library provides a degree
of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like
"this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...",
 makes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when
working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines;
the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's
there, optionally ( is another option for a more statically typed
flavor).
The right approach to object-orientation
Historically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This
doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however.
Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of
OO-like features.
That said, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to
discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of
interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms
of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability
to do true multiple dispatch
and you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips.
Built-in support for concurrency and parallelism
It wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for
concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many
ways, which are interleaved.
First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent
data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a
multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data
structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to
implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally
appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too
much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of
persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient
and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems.
Second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support
lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are
built-in mutable state units with atomic updates. Refs and transactions go further, implementing STM.
Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises,
futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities.
Finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in the
 module. It provides two useful things:
  1. Channels and Go -like functionality () which makes it
easy to work with safe concurrent queues and "share data by communicating".
  2. go-blocks with non-blocking primitives that make it possible
to write cooperative "green threads" with ease.
Finally, it's important to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic
exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in
the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless -
Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core
Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood.
On the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another
language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side
programming, among with some unique features like  for
callback-free concurrency.
This doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next
project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance
of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation,
Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows,
maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great!
If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming
languages.

items.title: Re: Riemann
items.author: _dain_
items.content:
A fun thing about living in Australia is that most things happen overnight, so reading the news in the morning is like a gacha game. You pick up the phone and scroll through notifications of world-historic events: elections won, wars begun, models released, conjectures proven or refuted. Today’s pull was a Discord notification saying: “they proved riemann :/”.

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that I tried to become familiar with all tools that I could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. I had us on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe.

Compare the above to Ayn Rand’s account of watching the launch of Apollo 11:

How do you descend from a state of pure exaltation?

What we had seen, in naked essentials—but in reality, not in a work of art—was the concretized abstraction of man’s greatness.

The meaning of the sight lay in the fact that when those dark red wings of fire flared open, one knew that one was not looking at a normal occurrence, but at a cataclysm which, if unleashed by nature, would have wiped man out of existence—and one knew also that this cataclysm was planned, unleashed, and by man, that this unimaginable power was ruled by power and, obediently serving his purpose, was making way for a slender, rising craft. One knew that this spectacle was not the product of inanimate nature, like some aurora borealis, or of chance, or of luck, that it was unmistakably human—with “human,” for once, meaning —that a purpose and a long, sustained, disciplined effort had gone to achieve this series of moments, and that man was succeeding, succeeding, succeeding! For once, if only for seven minutes, the worst among those who saw it had to feel—not “How small is man by the side of the Grand Canyon!”—but “How great is man and how safe is nature when he conquers it!”

Rand’s essay says: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.

It’s a collage of images of science, technology, history, cells, galaxies, the universe at the nanoscale and the exascale. And at the center there is a man, his hands grasping the controls. He wears a complicated expression: the weight of responsibility for the future, the weight of autonomy.

And I see this mural, and think: how great is Man! Our life is like a breath of air, we were beset by illness and hunger and cold, millions and hundreds of millions died in plagues. And yet we—sick, hungry, short-lived—learned the system of the world, crawled out of the caves, brought nature to heel, walked on the Moon. The last shall be first! And eyes that are clouded with age have seen the furthest stars, and the lives of a cell, and the worlds of Cantor and Hilbert: the invisible world that waited forever. We are dust and ashes, and yet our minds bestride the universe. How great is Man!

And when I read the Riemann announcement, when I read : humanity is not at the center. Claude is at the center. We are hidden in the margins, passive recipients of manna from Claude. How great is Claude! How noble in reason, how infinite in benevolence! The dancing star, the living word!

items.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains
items.author: mv4
items.content:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 6, 2026.
Spencer Platt | Getty Images

Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The turned negative for the year, and the entered correction territory alongside the .

The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73. The index was down 2.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to end at 6,910.39, while the blue-chip Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. Both the S&P 500 and Dow moved 10% below their closing records.

The plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.

Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each lost more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.

"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."

The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.

Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as and as well as others like and seeing gains. Walmart gained more than 1%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose around 1%.

"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.

For the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement.
